body: Probably important to know: that experimental flag was discontinued and is no longer being worked on, it'll likely be removed in the near future.
author: timneutkens

body:
Thanks!

Really? That flag is what enables SSR to work properly for tailwind apps in pages mode. You get a flash of unstyled content otherwise. Is there a preferred way of solving that? 

I opened this discussion https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/62777 to ask if there was some way of doing this in userland pre response but I don't think there is.

body:
After updating to `14.1.2` we got surprised by an issue - we have an async server action function in a file marked with `use server`. That function was calling another function in the same file that was not async, but was exported (turns out for no reason, not using it anywhere else). I didn't get any warnings from nextjs on this, but it absolutely broke the original function since the other fn was now returning a promise instead of it's original value. Removing `export` from the function definition fixed that - but this was certainly unexpected.

The new fix seems to be automatically converting all exported functions in a `use server` file to async with no warning. Is this like...a bug? As in, should I log it somewhere? It certainly feels like a breaking change (since it did break our production build), but I'm not sure what to do with that information. If "do nothing" is the answer that's fine, I just wanted to bring it up.

> After updating to `14.1.2` we got surprised by an issue - we have an async server action function in a file marked with `use server`. That function was calling another function in the same file that was not async, but was exported (turns out for no reason, not using it anywhere else). I didn't get any warnings from nextjs on this, but it absolutely broke the original function since the other fn was now returning a promise instead of it's original value. Removing `export` from the function definition fixed that - but this was certainly unexpected.
> 
> The new fix seems to be automatically converting all exported functions in a `use server` file to async with no warning. Is this like...a bug? As in, should I log it somewhere? It certainly feels like a breaking change (since it did break our production build), but I'm not sure what to do with that information. If "do nothing" is the answer that's fine, I just wanted to bring it up.

Same here. I noticed the issue by an unexpected returned value, otherwise there was no errors or warnings. I was able to debug the issue by logging the result returned by server action and realize that it actually returns a promise even though the function is synchronous. Apparently all functions placed in a "use server" file are automatically turned into async functions, even though definitions are sync. In my opinion it was the missing piece for use server files and definitely a great improvement. 

But we need an Eslint check/error for sync functions placed in use server files.
author: mertafor

body:
Hey everyone, thanks for all your feedback!

## Tl;DR

`"use server"` **requires** the functions to be async. If they are not, they will be converted to async functions.

So, instead of silently converting your sync functions to be async (breaks type checking), here we're directly showing errors and ask you to make them async in the first place.

## Details

> it breaks `React.cache`

Please give https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/62860#issuecomment-1978730839 a read - `React.cache` will not do anything when it's called inside a Server Action.

> but it absolutely broke the original function since the other fn was now returning a promise instead of it's original value

As per this PR description, async functions and sync functions that return promises are fundamentally different things:

```js
const f = async () => { throw 1; return 1 }
const g = () => { throw 1; return Promise.resolve(1) }
```

> The new fix seems to be automatically converting all exported functions in a use server file to async with no warning. Is this like...a bug?

Again, as mentioned in the PR description, "Because the underlying network calls are always asynchronous, 'use server' can only be used on async functions." (https://react.dev/reference/react/use-server) that's a **requirement**. Previously that's not ensured which was a bug and this PR fixes it.

> But we need an Eslint check/error for sync functions placed in use server files.

This would be great, but it's difficult to ensure the type statically. Also in TS `async () => {}` and `() => Promise` are considered the same type but they're actually different things.

> Agree. It also breaks the use of Zod for validating the input of Server Actions (this worked before)

Agreed that this is annoying. I'll see if there are any other work arounds.

body:
Can you clarify this? I think in many cases people would prefer up-to-date data than a perfect scroll match. If you do end up going this route, could you at least make it opt-in for users? I'd rather Next.js not make assumptions about what we want when it comes to data freshness.
> This also doesn't change back/forward caching behavior to ensure things like scroll restoration etc still work nicely.
author: jrnxf

body:
@jrnxf this matches the decision that was posted as part of the [original proposal](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/54075#discussioncomment-6754339) -- copied below for convenience:

> Back/forward navigation will still preserve the cache, it does not invalidate this cache in order to mirror bfcache, based on the replies most folks said this is fine.
> What I’m expecting is that others might want to do an update on back navigation based on expiring of staletime too, so Sebastian and I discussed potentially having a way to do the stale-while-revalidate pattern built-in for back navigations. The current default is still preferable for most applications though as it ensures scroll position is always where you were before, instead of feeling broken as items shift around on the page, so we’ll have to figure out if this is something we’d want to have on back navigation and how to opt-in to that, overall it’s not a blocker for adding staletime in my opinion based on most replies saying the current behavior for back/forward is fine.

This is an experimental flag, so its behavior might change based on feedback and testing. Disabling the router bfcache might be a separate flag entirely.

What traffic do you expect for including a tool?
When does it make sense to request an add again?

What is a CVE?

Contains a high severity Common Vulnerability and Exposure (CVE).

Remove or replace dependencies that include known high severity CVEs. Consumers can use dependency overrides or npm audit fix --force to remove vulnerable dependencies.

What is a deprecated package?

The maintainer of the package marked it as deprecated. This could indicate that a single version should not be used, or that the package is no longer maintained and any new vulnerabilities will not be fixed.

Research the state of the package and determine if there are non-deprecated versions that can be used, or if it should be replaced with a new, supported solution.

Take a deeper look at the dependency

Take a moment to review the security alert above. Review the linked package source code to understand the potential risk. Ensure the package is not malicious before proceeding. If you're unsure how to proceed, reach out to your security team or ask the Socket team for help at support [AT] socket [DOT] dev.

Remove the package

If you happen to install a dependency that Socket reports as Known Malware you should immediately remove it and select a different dependency. For other alert types, you may may wish to investigate alternative packages or consider if there are other ways to mitigate the specific risk posed by the dependency.

Mark a package as acceptable risk

To ignore an alert, reply with a comment starting with @SocketSecurity ignore followed by a space separated list of ecosystem/package-name@version specifiers. e.g. @SocketSecurity ignore npm/foo@1.0.0 or ignore all packages with @SocketSecurity ignore-all

body:
I am not certain whether declaring the compiled module in next/types is correct, since in all other instances (postcss-next-font, css-minimizer-plugin.ts), postcss and its types were imported directly.

Also, ideally, I would have liked to export the configuration type `type PostCssPluginsConfig = { plugins: CssPluginCollection }` for postcss.config.js somewhere available to end users, but I couldn't find a location that made sense (for IDE intellisense). The only export Next.js has for /build is `next/babel`, and none of the exports really make sense for this. Maybe adding an export like `next/webpack` may be useful (may also go hand-in-hand with the LightningCSS support)?

body:
Hi, first of all, thanks a lot for your efforts for this feature. I imagine that implementing it properly requires much consideration. I appreciate your goal to limit the scope in order to ship a working solution soon. That being said, I'd like to comment on:

> So we won't allow importing additional .ts files beyond types inside of this file initially.

Our config file has some logic that it shares with a custom production server. So the config file exports a function and imports a few other shared configuration files, functions and also types. This complexity is the reason why we've written it in TypeScript. (Previously, we had called an internal Next build function directly from our TypeScript build script, but of course, using a non-public API might break with every Next update.)

We're fine with compiling next.config.ts and its dependencies ourselves if you consider this case to be rare or undesirable. Still I imagine that many folks would like to use a next.config.ts precisely because they need to import some other TypeScript logic. So I'd appreciate if you still consider supporting a "full" next.config.ts at some time in the future.

body:
@glennsc Thanks for sharing this!

Unfortunately, it's unlikely that we'll add this into this section because we're lacking mentions of other hosting providers that work with Next.js.
author: samcx

body: Oh! @samcx Are there other hosting providers that work at this managed level with the new server-side features?  It seems like you would want to inform Next.js users of their deployment options besides Vercel.
author: glennsc

body:
@glennsc Yes there are! But, since we don't extensively test other hosting providers ourselves, it's difficult to accurately say what the exact extent the support is.

The problem if we started adding these sections, we'd have to maintain all of them to make sure they're up to date (very likely to get stale if we don't extensively test this ourselves). I think the better option is to leave it to SEO for other users to find for hosting (full-fledged features or not) outside of Vercel.

body:
Thanks for the PR for ESM support @phanect and for the review and merge @huozhi 🙌 

I can confirm that [`next@14.2.0-canary.25`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v14.2.0-canary.25) does have support for the following ESM configurations 🎉

1. CommonJS project + `postcss.config.mjs` in ESM format
2. ESM project + `postcss.config.js` in ESM format

More details here:

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/34448#issuecomment-2002513315

body:
A few things on this
- .next/cache doesn't exist in the builder phase and only shows up when the app starts. 
- Without explicitly making the directory in the Dockerfile, you get the error I've identified. 
- If you don't modify the permissions of the cache folder (changing owner/user is not enough), then you'll get the same error on the creation of .next/cache/images

If your not seeing any of these issue, then I would asked what version of next are you using, and are you statically generating any pages? 

Navigating to a statically generated page throws the errors in the logs.

body:
This is a nice item to have in the docs but should we not have the scroll behavior work to where it scrolls to the top of the page? That seems to be the way pages have worked for decades now and therefore it is a bit more intuitive (comfortable) for users.

Another solution could be to set allow devs to set the scroll position to the top of {children} with a prop {scrollChildren}, or something like that, and have the default scroll to the top of the page.
author: guylepage3
samcx

body:
I would have to disagree. Users for the past 40 years expect to go to the top of the page. If you have a Next app loaded in your browser close the browser and come back to it the page refreshes, and goes not to the top of the page but to what would appear to the user, a random spot on the page. In fact, the user doesn't remember that there was content above the {children} content.

I've had two potential investors tell me this about my app. My work around for this is to place a small modal in the top right corner to let users know that, hey 👋🏻, there might be content above this spot on the page. Please try scrolling up. Possibly the worst UX I've ever had to implement.
author: guylepage3

body: @samcx See reply above
author: guylepage3

body:
>  goes not to the top of the page but to what would appear to the user, a random spot on the page.

cc @guylepage3  Is there a lot of static content within your Layout that would cause the `{children}` to be not visible in the viewport (often)? I would recommend you move those to your Page instead so your Page is always in the viewport → scroll always scrolls to the top of the route.
author: samcx

body: @samcx tried that to be honest. I tried a lot of things. But this seems to be a major issue. I've come across 5 issues on here where people are trying to figure out what's wrong and a lot of comments on StackOverflow and other places. I actually don't know if this is for sure the issue

body:
> One thing that was a bit surprising was that sharp was not present in node_modules/sharp, but I guess that's a detail of how pnpm does hoisting of optional dependencies:

That's how pnpm works. You can `shamefully-hoist` if you want pnpm to behave like npm and hoist dependencies up.

> Looking forward to the stable release (currently assuming this will be in the next minor):

It will will likely be `next@15.0.0` since dropping yarn@1 could be considered a breaking change. I suppose it could be minor if we think that yarn@1 usage is nearing zero but we would have to look at telemetry (not sure if we currently collect that data). Or we could consider it non-breaking since yarn@1 has a workaround but that might be painful to add the `--ignore-engines` flag.

author: samcx

body:
Introduced Variables for Configuration: The script now uses max_retries and sleep_interval variables to define the maximum number of retries and the interval between retries, respectively. This makes it easier to configure these values without modifying the core logic of the script.

Added Validation for NODE_VERSION: A check has been added to ensure that the NODE_VERSION environment variable is set before proceeding with the installation. If it's not set, the script exits with an error message, thereby preventing any unintended behavior due to an unset version.

Encapsulated Node.js Installation Logic in a Function: The Node.js installation command has been encapsulated within an install_node function. This improves the modularity of the script, making the retry logic cleaner and more readable by separating the installation-specific code from the control flow.

Enhanced Logging for Better Debuggability: The script now includes more informative logging. It logs each attempt to install Node.js, indicating the current retry count out of the maximum allowed retries. This enhancement aids in debugging by providing clearer insight into the script's execution flow.

Structured Retry Logic Using a For Loop: The retry logic has been restructured using a for loop with a C-style syntax. This approach provides a clearer, more conventional structure for implementing the retry mechanism, making the script easier to understand and maintain.

Final Failure Message: If all retries fail, the script outputs a message indicating the failure to install Node.js after the specified number of attempts, providing clear feedback that the installation process did not succeed.

body:
Hey @agadzik! happy to see such an integration, we at Playwright are currently in the process of doing something on the Playwright level and comparing different approaches, like e.g. [ssr](https://github.com/playwright-community/ssr/) (which is similar to the Next.js experimental feature except it has a webServer per worker and WS as a transport in between instead of http-proxy).

I saw also @dvoytenko's initial work in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/52520 which introduced it which looks awesome.

Would be curious about your experience with this integration, especially having a global webserver vs. webServer per worker. Do you plan to move it out of experimental soon? We might add something similar to Playwright, so I would be more than happy to talk!

body:
@remorses 

> Awesome! I wonder if there are more opportunities like this to improve cold start performance

From time spent on importing
```
  14ms node_modules/next/dist/compiled/watchpack/watchpack.js
```
also caught my attention as something that doesn't seem like it would be needed to run production server (this seems more like something for dev server to watch source files and recompile them when users make edits), but this one had much smaller cost so  I didn't yet look into it as I do have other opportunities to look into first (more on my side of things than Next.js) - but maybe this is something someone else can look into as well?

This changed just seemed like real low hanging fruit

Of course there is also whole other part which is actual initialization of the server (after it is imported) that could be profiled? I did see open-telemetry instrumentation across Next.js codebase as well, so potentially that could yield some insights that would be easier to read than something like CPU profile

@ryota-murakami Can you make sure the `text-balance` class gets updated to `text-wrap` in the templates as well?

E.g., https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/create-next-app/templates/app-tw/ts/app/page.tsx
author: samcx

body:
@samcx Before tailwindCSS@3.4.0, they have no class name 'text-balance' so next templetes defined `text-balance` class as `text-wrap: balance;` rule.  
But now,  tailwindCSS has 'text-balance' classname as a exact same rule `text-wrap: balance;` .

I recorded that ensure  TailwindCSS native `text-balance` applied  `text-wrap: balance;` rule without custom defined `text-balance` in `@layer`.


https://github.com/vercel/next.js/assets/5501268/5843ac26-55f2-4b45-bbd8-b606d8eb3faf

body:
Heh sorry, that was a bit terse :sweat_smile: 

I'm trying to reproduce the error message I got yesterday, but weirdly, I can't reproduce the exact error message now - instead, I suddenly get a 404 response on a request to the route handler that calls MJML (and then sends an email with its output), and quite a few of the following logs:

```
./node_modules/mjml-core/lib/helpers/mjmlconfig.js
Critical dependency: the request of a dependency is an expression
```

Whereas I recall that yesterday, before I added `mjml` to my `serverComponentsExternalPackages`, I got an error message about a require call to `uglify-js` (which MJML can use on the HTML it generates for an email) failing, but I don't recall the exact error message, unfortunately.

body: @anatoliik-lyft Hmm not exactly sure these are different. Is it possible to further clarify the difference of these word choices?
author: samcx

body:
> @anatoliik-lyft Hmm not exactly sure these are different. Is it possible to further clarify the difference of these word choices?

@samcx Thanks for the review! Sure! The revision clarifies that the cookie doesn’t change the accept-language header but takes precedence when determining language settings. It's about prioritizing the cookie's value over the header's, not modifying the header itself.

**before**
```
Next.js supports overriding the accept-language header with a `NEXT_LOCALE=the-locale` cookie.
```
**after**
```
Next.js allows setting a `NEXT_LOCALE=the-locale` cookie, which takes priority over the accept-language header.
```

body:
> `array.every()` already short circuits, so the worse case is checking each format once
> 
> ```js
> [0,1,2,3,4].every((_, i) => {console.log(i); return false}) // prints 0
> ```
> 
> Did you benchmark this before/after to see if there is any measurable difference?

Minimizing function calls can shave off a few milliseconds, but I'm skeptical about its impact compared to the time consumed by the image optimizer (sharp, squoosh) itself, which is significantly more substantial.
author: SukkaW

body:
> Minimizing function calls can shave off a few milliseconds

I'm seeing the exact same time on my machine comparing existing code to your new code, which is why I'm asking if you're seeing a difference.

### Before
```
 PASS  test/unit/image-optimizer/detect-content-type.test.ts
  detectContentType
    ✓ should return jpg (2 ms)
    ✓ should return png
    ✓ should return webp
    ✓ should return svg
    ✓ should return avif
    ✓ should return icon (1 ms)
```

### After

```
 PASS  test/unit/image-optimizer/detect-content-type.test.ts
  detectContentType
    ✓ should return jpg (2 ms)
    ✓ should return png
    ✓ should return webp
    ✓ should return svg
    ✓ should return avif (1 ms)
    ✓ should return icon
```

I think PRs that address "perf" should have the benchmarks to backup that claim.
author: styfle

body: I guess content type detection is not a hot path anyway, I am closing the issue now.

body:
@dvoytenko Re our slack convo: To clarify in what cases trace metadata should be propagated to the client:

- **tldr:** Effectively only for pageloads or hard navigations.
- **Not** for any statically generated pages, as the "cached" trace data would be picked up by all clients and create huge and unusable traces.
- **Not** for any PPR content. (same reason as static pages)
- **Not** for soft navigations. Traces for navigations originate from the client and do not need to be propagated back.

I added tests for all of the above.

I think moving forward we need to get clearance two things:
- The naming of the meta tags. Imo, this can be `_next-trace-data-*` for now as the option is experimental and we can update later if we find a better name.
- Whether what I did in `makeGetServerInsertedHTML()` makes sense or whether this needs to live somewhere else.
author: lforst

body:
> * **Not** for any statically generated pages, as the "cached" trace data would be picked up by all clients and create huge and unusable traces.
> * **Not** for any PPR content. (same reason as static pages)

This sounds reasonable. But how does your code avoid having these values produced in these modes?

P.S. We actually produce trace references for both static and PPR. But we are not using them as parent traces - that would indeed make the parent traces huge and not useful. We simply use them as links/tags for other traces to add. It reads like this: "this trace was produced by a page which was originally statically generated".
author: dvoytenko

body:
@dvoytenko Thanks for giving this another pass!

> > * **Not** for any statically generated pages, as the "cached" trace data would be picked up by all clients and create huge and unusable traces.
> > * **Not** for any PPR content. (same reason as static pages)
> 
> This sounds reasonable. But how does your code avoid having these values produced in these modes?

Currently, we don't explicitly check for PPR/SSG, but I _believe_ the code path where we would generate the `<meta>` tags is simply not executed for PPR and static pages. In theory, the tests I added verify this 🤔 ([1](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64256/files#diff-c8dda8307d78c09f1f8b30c67ca78de6d5982132e6c161ea041e41ad7556cf97R48), [2](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64256/files#diff-c8dda8307d78c09f1f8b30c67ca78de6d5982132e6c161ea041e41ad7556cf97R82), [3](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64256/files#diff-c8dda8307d78c09f1f8b30c67ca78de6d5982132e6c161ea041e41ad7556cf97R11)). Maybe someone working on the Next.js team working on this part of the code can confirm. If you feel like it's a good idea, I can also explicitly check for SSG and PPR and not inject the meta tags, however, I would lean towards not doing that because it would essentially be dead code assuming the code path is actually not hit.

The point about generating traces for static content also makes complete sense 👍 I assume you're using that already to track Next.js compile speed? We should just make sure that those traces do not leak into production monitoring, but I think we are aligned on that point and the tests already test for it.

body:
After this PR I can't start a Next.js server from Playwright anymore. I don't even use the `experimental-test` command, just `next dev` (configured in the Playwright config). It works fine in version `14.3.0-canary.21`.

> Error: http://localhost:3000 is already used, make sure that nothing is running on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.

It works if I set `reuseExistingServer` but this sounds like a regression nonetheless.

cc @wyattjoh @dvoytenko
author: kevva

body:
Interesting, this seems to be fault of Playwright's `defineConfig` merge behavior. We now include a default `webServer` configuration so you don't have to specify it. 

For now, unless you're specifying something different than our default in `webServer`, can you remove it from your config? That should restore functionality.
author: Ethan-Arrowood

body: @Ethan-Arrowood, I can confirm that seems to have fixed the issue. Works in `v14.3.0-canary.27` and onwards :+1:.

What version of ESLint is Next.js using? Maybe the APIs are different?
author: coltonehrman

body: @coltonehrman It doesn't seem like that was updated → https://eslint.org/docs/v8.x/use/command-line-interface#--report-unused-disable-directives-severity. Next.js is still on v8.
author: samcx

body:
> @coltonehrman It doesn't seem like that was updated → https://eslint.org/docs/v8.x/use/command-line-interface#--report-unused-disable-directives-severity. Next.js is still on v8.

The docs don't seem to be in sync with the behavior then _(or even perhaps the version of ESLint Next.js is using has a bug)_. The flag that is suppose to be boolean doesn't appear to support a boolean value when ran and results in an error. However, as you pointed out, it does appear that the `*-severity` flag should be used instead. Should we update Next.js to use the latest version of ESLint and then verify the flags again with the latest behavior?
author: coltonehrman

body: @coltonehrman I'll push up the changes to make this `--report-unused-disable-directives-severity` with the correct choices `['error', null, 'off', 'warn']`. We should update the eslint version in another PR (if there isn't already a PR for that).
author: samcx

body: @samcx Just out of curiosity, what is the reason for taking over control of the lint command via Next.js vs passing through options to the underlying tool (ie: ESLint)? I feel like this would cause more issues and be harder to maintain.
author: coltonehrman

body: @coltonehrman That's a good question—I think the idea is we give you good defaults. So when you simply do `next lint`, you don't have to worry about adding your own CLI options.

body:
> Do you have an ETA that will release this in a patch?

@huozhi The PR I linked in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64467#issuecomment-2054129027 is what I believe surfaced this bug (it's a step for Material UI toward exporting server components). The last stable release of Material UI is [v5.15.15](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/releases/tag/v5.15.15) which was 16 days ago. I see two options:

- We wait, at this point, it is a matter of time before the problem is gone if I can trust: https://github.com/mui/material-ui/issues/41865#issuecomment-2054932000.
- Material UI revert https://github.com/mui/material-ui/pull/40663 in v5 (and keep it in v6), we do a release within a week, which probably makes the most sense only if the next Next.js stable release is scheduled to be in >4 weeks. 

cc @DiegoAndai
author: oliviertassinari

body:
There're still a few files need to tackle such as the barrel files in mui/material, e.g. [mui-material/src/Container/index.js](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/blob/next/packages/mui-material/src/Container/index.js).

The issue is that when you use `"use client"` with `export *`, we can't analyze properly about the used exports atm, so that lead to the errors user reported. I already fixed in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64681 and leave more explanation there. We can wait for the next patch release of Next.js to solve it but the bundle will still include more unused stuffs which is not ideal. So just wanna flag that would be better to remove more client directives in mui and only apply them to the component where we need.
author: huozhi

Hey! (by sheer coincidence) we [opened a PR](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/pull/41956) yesterday to remove all "`"use client"` with `export *`" occurrences, which would land in v6 alpha. We could consider cherry-picking it to v5.

I rephrase @oliviertassinari's question: is the next Next.js stable release scheduled to be in >4 weeks? And will that include https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64681? With this info we could plan our next steps on the MUI side.

body:
> The issue is that when you use "use client" with export *, we can't analyze properly about the used exports atm

@huozhi I'm confused by this one. Is this a client/server bundle issue, a tree-shaking issue, or something else? I can blame the error:

> Error: It's currently unsupported to use "export *" in a client boundary. Please use named exports instead.

with https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/46171 as the origin of when the error message was added. 

> atm we cannot statically analyze all the exports from this the boundary, unless we can apply barrel file optimization for every import which could slow down speed.

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64681. So I guess it's why it was working before .

> When we found the mixing client entry module like that, we treat it as a CJS client module and include all the bundle in client like before what we have the client components import optimization.

This seems to be OK, what's the downside of doing this?
author: oliviertassinari

body: It's a tree-shaking issue, it will work properly once the fix on canary is out on stable release. I mean if we want to get best optimization for v5, it's good to remove the "use client" in barrel file where it contains `export *`. It doesn't effect much mostly the subpath import cases like `import Container from '@mui/material/Container/Container'`.

This doesn't work. We have some modules that have more specific types internally because we have the types available as a dependency (e.g. Webpack). When published, the Webpack dependency is stripped and replaced with a looser definition based on what we assume is actually emitted. I don't think TypeScript supports this pattern outside of `@internal` annotations.

`compiled.d.ts` isn't even referenced by any emitted declaration at the moment while the non-published `misc.d.ts` is.

Need to dig deeper why some declarations are emitted in the first place.

body:
It's because in that testing project we have a `middleware.js`

So a request goes like req -> middleware -> request handler. And it will pass through the handling in `next-server` twice. We logged in both middleware phase and the final request handler phase. So we checked the header if the 1st request is for middleware. Then when you request a path like `GET /foo` you won't see it's logged in next-server twice.

@eps1lon Thanks for the feedback, in terms of motivation: it's very common for scaffolding/npx scripts to provide such a flag, i.e. angular, vite, astro all either have a flag to skip `npm install` or not run it at all(vite). Similar goes for `cargo`, `gonew` etc.

As for the concrete use case: in [Project IDX](https://idx.dev/) we support Nextjs starter templates and not having this `--skip-install` option makes NextJS templates take too long to instantiate and not caching friendly(where we can instantiate the template ahead of time and copy files into place for the user at creation time). Otoh, once the initial scaffold is ready we can start launching the Dev Environment and have `npm install` run when the user has access to the IDE as opposed to being blocked by the `npm install`. wdyt?

body:
> This change does not look correct to me. The intent of next-polyfill-module and next-polyfill-nomodule is to ensure compat with the supported browsers: https://nextjs.org/docs/architecture/supported-browsers. These browsers are specifically chosen as they're the cutoff point of `module`/`nomodule` support (ES Modules support). So the built-in polyfill that are loaded in all browsers, and the polyfills that are only loaded in browsers that don't support ES Modules, are specifically tuned to support the APIs that the ES Modules browsers had at the time, not to load all polyfills, as that would mean Next.js will forever keep increasing the polyfill size whenever new browser features are added, that's not something we want, i.e. we don't want to have to load a polyfill for `toReversed` in all browsers because the older version of ES Modules browsers also doesn't have it.
> 
> Our recommendation for these newer features is to pull in the polyfills as you need them / want to use them. In this case you need to load the `toReversed` polyfill for all browsers, even ones that support it, as there is no way to conditionally load it like `nomodule`.
> 
> Hope that clarifies 🙏

Thanks for responding. To make sure I understand it correctly, since these `to*()` methods are only available post-module era and we don't want next.js to grow its polyfill size permanently whenever there are new API available, it would rather be better for us to create custom polyfilling? 

If so, I can understand that although it's ambiguous to say that next.js supports Chrome 64+ with zero-config, we still need to polyfill `to*()` to actually use them to prevent polyfilling size to grow indefinitely.

However, this leads to another issue: in https://nextjs.org/docs/architecture/supported-browsers#custom-polyfills, it says `In this case, you should add a top-level import for the specific polyfill you need in your Custom <App> or the individual component.` But with App router `/app`, there's no `<App>`. How do we do custom polyfill in this case? I have tried the following commits in my repo, but none of them works:
- https://github.com/RaenonX-PokemonSleep/pokemon-sleep-ui/commit/d4ce3c1862ed5cef7ddcb1e83b37ece66ab0300a
- https://github.com/RaenonX-PokemonSleep/pokemon-sleep-ui/commit/2440e74979ba8a621bd6c2e5bf42151fc3e890f0
- https://github.com/RaenonX-PokemonSleep/pokemon-sleep-ui/commit/6607658c6065bad0731725e11f73f9cdcaa6cd21

body:
It was just a suggestion, because the general idea behind environment variables is to avoid hardcoding values. However, I've seen some cases where NEXT_PUBLIC environment variables were used in a way that exposed critical information. 

While it's common sense to avoid insecure practices that could reveal sensitive data, some people might mistakenly believe using environment variables is inherently safe.

body:
Hey @remcohaszing, thanks for the PR. Could you provide more context for these changes? E.g. did recommendations change, or is this personal preference?

I guess because useMDXComponents is not exposed to the user, therefore you can never pass components?
author: delbaoliveira

body:
Nothing changed. `useMDXComponents()` was never passed any arguments. `MDXProvider` from `@mdx-js/react` [does pass components](https://github.com/mdx-js/mdx/blob/2.3.0/packages/react/lib/index.js#L76) to `useMDXComponents()`, but compiled MDX files don’t. The `mdx-components` file replaces `@mdx-js/react`. I imagine this caused some confusion initially.

The change to declare `MDXProvidedComponents` is based on https://github.com/mdx-js/mdx-analyzer?#mdxprovidedcomponents.

Semi-related: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/59693, https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/62503
author: remcohaszing

body:
@remcohaszing this one has tripped me up before too, but it does take arguments. 

1. This follows [the MDX spec for `useMDXComponents`](https://mdxjs.com/packages/react/#usemdxcomponentscomponents).
2. We updated the MDX docs last week to clarify what is happening → #63568. It has to do with ["global"](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/configuring/mdx#global-styles-and-components) and ["local"](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/configuring/mdx#local-styles-and-components) components.

I am going to close this PR based on the above. We can reopen if we find a need to.

Good catch, let me add that back and update this branch shortly. In the mean time, what would be the right way to run just a subset of the e2e tests locally? For example, from the [original PR's test checks](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/59282/checks), only these ones failed:

- [test dev (2/4) / build](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/7179317638/job/19549288692?pr=59282)
- [test ppr dev (1/4) / build](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/7179317638/job/19549295322?pr=59282)
- [test ppr prod (2/4) / build](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/7179317638/job/19549297447?pr=59282)

I see the test dev (1 through 4) processes are defined here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v14.3.0-canary.30/.github/workflows/build_and_test.yml#L287-L300 - so I tried running this command locally:

```
NEXT_TEST_MODE=dev node run-tests.js --timings -g 2/4 -c 8 --type development
```
(replacing TEST_CONCURRENCY with 8 since it's specified in the `env` section further up in the file)

That's running now for the past ~15 minutes still ongoing. I'm guessing there's a `-- --matchingTests opentelemetry` type of argument I need to include to limit which ones get run? 

I can't fully add back the `it('should handle client-side navigation', async () => { ... })` test because the supporting helper functions use `traceFile` from the ./constants file, but that value got removed a couple months back: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/62120/files#diff-95fdfa81f6699cf4ad4345cd01cc66ae151d91091ddf3f5ea4f04dd714c49f1b - is it safe to re-add it to that file? 

```
export const traceFile = 'otel-trace.txt'
```

For the test "should handle client-side navigation", it's essentially a snapshot test. I ran the test first expecting nothing, reviewed the traces and was happy with what I got. I saw some changes in theses files last time, so there might be new/modified traces too. Last commit I just pushed is as close as I've been to get everything passing. 
```
pnpm testheadless test/e2e/opentelemetry/opentelemetry.test.ts
```
Running that locally shows `2 failed, 25 passed, 27 total`

The 2 failed ones are just
```
opentelemetry › incoming context propagation › app router › should handle client-side navigation
opentelemetry › root context › app router › should handle client-side navigation
```

And it looks like the issue is just contained to the parentTraceId value:

![image](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/assets/967811/c1b458d5-b890-46e3-8fc5-cca77af90c6c)

What might be going awry in that test? @dvoytenko I want to loop you in on this since I see you introduced that `expectTrace` function a couple months back as part of https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/62120
author: PatNeedham

body: For the `root context › app router` path invocation of that test, it looks like the value received as `"parentId": undefined,` in all places while the expected value was `"parentId": "<random-id>",`.

body:
Would also like to see this land. For now we're using an OTEL span processor to reduce cardinality but it's less than ideal because we lose route information

```yaml
  span/nextjs:
    include:
      attributes:
      - key: next.span_type
        value: (BaseServer\.handleRequest|AppRender\.fetch)
      match_type: regexp
    name:
      to_attributes:
        rules:
        - ^(RSC|fetch)?.?(GET|POST|PUT) (?P<url>.+)$
```

What is an install script?

Install scripts are run when the package is installed. The majority of malware in npm is hidden in install scripts.

Packages should not be running non-essential scripts during install and there are often solutions to problems people solve with install scripts that can be run at publish time instead.

Take a deeper look at the dependency

Take a moment to review the security alert above. Review the linked package source code to understand the potential risk. Ensure the package is not malicious before proceeding. If you're unsure how to proceed, reach out to your security team or ask the Socket team for help at support [AT] socket [DOT] dev.

Remove the package

If you happen to install a dependency that Socket reports as Known Malware you should immediately remove it and select a different dependency. For other alert types, you may may wish to investigate alternative packages or consider if there are other ways to mitigate the specific risk posed by the dependency.

Mark a package as acceptable risk

To ignore an alert, reply with a comment starting with @SocketSecurity ignore followed by a space separated list of ecosystem/package-name@version specifiers. e.g. @SocketSecurity ignore npm/foo@1.0.0 or ignore all packages with @SocketSecurity ignore-all

author: jaysoo

body:
Could you please merge this as a hotfix/isolated fix once the tests pass? The current behavior for `build` is definitely broken in my opinion.

If a user or some other runner starts running `next build` and immediately cancels it, the process exits successfully (0).

However, nothing which was promised by the `next build` command was produced. There is no built Next.js application. No code was compiled. It's not ready to be deployed.

So the Next CLI really needs to be honest here and tell the user/ other runner that the command was indeed not successful because it was cancelled.

There may very well be a wider issue but it has taken longer to address. Being aware of and addressing the wider issue does not have to delay fixing the specific behavior which is broken for the `next build` command now. The work done in this PR would still have to be done as part of addressing the wider issue. 

Thanks!

body:
FYI there's some issue with our vendoring strategy. Having React installed here shouldn't affect our tests since App Router must use the bundled React version not the installed one.

The reason this PR fixes it, is that PNPM auto-installs peer dependencies of `next`. So now the test uses `react@18.2.0` instead of experimental. Both are wrong but only installing experimental breaks the test.

I've been trying to fix using installed React in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64806 with no luck so far.

Any help needed?
author: MalekBouba

body:
> Hi, could you add a test case where this is failing?

I'm encountering this exact failure while trying to implement a micro-frontends app using Turbo & NextJs rewriting feature (via middlewares).

I needed to implement a routing system that check both for auth and micro-app availability and handle a decent redirection/error page.

All is good and I succeeded to get a chain of middleware that work in harmony and did what's needed but unfortunately not the webpack's HMR. The related socket keeps failing due to this (bind "undefined") issue. Which offcourse affects 📉 hugely our DX.

After hours of digging, It seems like the ws upgrade query did it. It keeps returning http error (produced by the use case code fail), then, it retries without any success.. after around a minute of retries, it refresh the window automatically.

Finally, When I forced the suggested code by @Talentaa  in `apps/main/node_modules/next/dist/server/base-server.js`, the HMR socket works again, HMR works and the stack DX rises again 📈.

Possible related PRs & issues [#31515](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/31515#pullrequestreview-980899073) [#23147](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/23147)
author: MalekBouba

body:
Excited to see work on native Node steams happening! 

I'm maintaining an app at work migrating from a homegrown `renderToString` based framework in Node to Next (`pages` router), and we noticed what we suspect is some unnecessary overhead from using Node's web stream implementation (via `renderToReadableStream`) vs native streams (via `renderToPipeableStream`).

Happy to offer some feedback on performance from a large Production app if/when this work lands.

> FYI we've replaced taskr is being replaced with using Turborepo: #64825

Thanks for sharing it. `taskr` is still being used there but it's being cached by Turborepo. I'll add that to this PR.

Note that I replaced `taskr` to resolve modules for ncc in a ESM environment. It's also a considerably old library that hasn't received an update in the last 7 years.

body:
@lfades this is ambitious! I previously failed to do something similar but ended up making a fixture to assert various vendoring strategies would work across all different kinds of package managers.

One of the problems with our tests is they produce tarballs and package managers don't actually install from tarballs with the exact same semantics as they do with package names/urls. This caused my tests to all pass while failing in the real world after publishing.

I made this little test bench and came up with a strategy that works for all major package managers and tested using veredaccio to simulate a real package install. I haven't documented it well but LMK if you want to discuss it and see if it is relevant to this work

https://github.com/gnoff/vendor-strategy
author: gnoff

body:
@gnoff After finishing most of the work of implementing `@next/vendored` I'm actually not that happy with it. There's a considerable amount of breaking changes which make this PR very hard to review. My first iteration was to use a nested `node_modules` instead of `@next/vendored` as that would make the transition easier for all the internal stuff that depends on those packages being inside the next package while still allowing the `next` package to be compatible with package.json `exports`, which was my initial motivation in making all of this.

But honestly this looks like a nightmare to review so I'm more inclined into closing the PR and maybe try again with incremental changes. I'm also considering that instead of having a `@next/vendored` package we could instead have one package for every vendored dependency. That should make it easier to handle the types and exports of every package, by more closely matching how they work in npm (and automate all of this).
author: lfades

body: Closing the PR for now, this is too big of a change to test properly in a single PR. It could be nice to have this changes but with a better plan where this can be properly reviewed.

Oh, looks like I still haven't been able to avoid the CodeSandbox caching behavior:

1. When visiting https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template?file=%2Fpackage.json, CodeSandbox redirects to [a devbox called `blazing-wood-go8s7s` without an owner](https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/blazing-wood-go8s7s?file=%2Fpackage.json) which includes a cached `package.json` with the pinned `14.3.0-canary.26` version of `next`

This cached devbox means the reproduction will still get a pinned, cached version of Next.js

Ives has confirmed problems with the behavior above - we'll investigate minimal ways to disable this caching behavior. (Ideally completely on the CodeSandbox side, but potentially also involving the config here)

Eg. first thoughts: Maybe some environment variable that I can use to avoid creation of this extra devbox, which caches the `package.json` with the pinned version, eg:

```bash
# Only run `pnpm update next` when the user has owner rights on the sandbox

It’s peculiar that `bunx create next-app` works for you at all, since It’s the only one that doesn’t for me. (`bun create X` works, `bunx create X` doesn’t)

That's not too surprising, as It’s not documented anywhere that it *should* work; `bunx create next-app` essentially looks for the `create` package and attempts to execute its `bin` script, passing `next-app` as an argument (which should fail).

Both `bunx create-next-app` and `bun create next-app` worked as expected on linux and macOS (using both zsh and bash), and on Windows 10/11 (using both CMD and powershell)

`bunx create next-app` doesn't work anywhere.

author: samcx

body:
@samcx Admittedly, finding the relevant documentation wasn't easy at first, but `npm create` is essentially an alias for [npm init](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/commands/npm-init) which in turn calls [npm exec](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/commands/npm-exec)

And as per `npm init`'s docs:
> `npm init <initializer>` can be used to set up a new or existing npm package.
`initializer` in this case is an npm package named `create-<initializer>`, which will be installed by [npm-exec](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/commands/npm-exec), and then have its main bin executed -- presumably creating or updating package.json and running any other initialization-related operations.
author: abdoufma

body: In other words: `npm create X`, `npm init X`, `npm exec create-X`, and `npx create-X` are all different ways to achieve the same outcome.

author: timneutkens

body:
Apologies in advance if this question has been answered elsewhere, at least in spirit. I am not familiar with next's release strategy.

It looks like this was first included in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v14.3.0-canary.23 Does that mean this change will only be in versions 14.3+? Are changes like this ever back-ported to previous major releases such as 13.x, for example? I'm guessing not, but I wanted to confirm. The codebase in which I am eager to consume this change is using 13.x right now, so I am trying to figure out what kind of version bump will be required to leverage these updates.

Thank you in advance!
author: SatsAllDay

body:
We cherry-pick commits from the canary branch to do patch releases on the 14.2 line, we don't backport these changes to 13.x currently.

You should be able to upgrade to Next.js 14, the only hard-breaking change we added in Next.js 14 is updating the minimum required Node.js version, which you should already be using Node.js 18 because 16 is end of life anyway.

body:
This work is awesome! Really excited for it and dove in this morning to try it out. A question I have is does this only work for dynamic routes? I made a reproduction of the issue I'm seeing here https://github.com/jer-k/parallel-routes. Copying in what I wrote in the README there. Also I can open a new issue if that is preferred

The structure of the above project has `@breadcrumbs/[...catchAll]/page.tsx` to capture the path for the breadcrumbs.

Then we have two sets of nested paths
* `[name]/[last]/page.tsx`
* `blog/[slug]/page.tsx`

When I visit `http://localhost:3000/jeremy/kreutzbender` I receive both params

```
rendering in @breadcrumbs / BreadcrumbSlot {
  params: { catchAll: [ 'jeremy', 'kreutzbender' ] },
  searchParams: {}
}
GET /jeremy/kreutzbender 200 in 937ms
```

Then when I visit `http://localhost:3000/blog/test` I do not get `blog` in the path params

```
rendering in @breadcrumbs / BreadcrumbSlot { params: { catchAll: [ 'test' ] }, searchParams: {} }
GET /blog/test 200 in 34ms
```

My question is whether this is in the intended behavior. If so, how would I build my breadcrumbs component
to incorporate `Blog` into it?
